1:
The interval between sin and rebuke is reckoned in months and treated as deliberate. Gill puts it at nine months or more, dating the visit just after the birth, when the thing had become public talk and the enemies of religion were full of it. Keil and Delitzsch say almost a whole year, fixing the point after the birth of the child begotten in adultery. Henry agrees on about nine months and adds that for anything the narrative shows the sin lay unrepented of. On his condition through that silence they also agree. Gill has his heart hardened, his graces dormant, the joys of salvation taken away and his communion with God broken off, with perhaps some pangs that quickly went off. Henry puts it in a figure: his comforts suspended, his harp out of tune, his soul like a tree in winter that has life in the root only.

Whether he had repented privately before Nathan came is genuinely disputed. Gill reports that some think he had — acknowledging his sin privately, receiving a sense of pardon, and composing two penitential psalms before this visit, Nathan being sent only to draw out a public repentance, expressed in a third psalm afterwards (Psalm 51:1). Henry denies the premise flatly. He would willingly hope that David's heart smote him and that he lamented in secret, and yet he holds it certain that during those nine months he penned no psalms at all. Keil and Delitzsch turn one of those psalms to the opposite purpose: it describes, on their reading, not a repentance already made but the state of David's heart through that very period, and his sufferings while he tried to conceal the crime (Psalm 32:3).

Why God waited at all is answered with two distinct purposes. Keil and Delitzsch give both: the fruit of the sin had first to be brought to light, so that the sinner could neither deny nor conceal what he had done, and God would first break his unbroken heart by the torture of his own conscience, preparing it to feel the prophet's reproaches. Wesley reads the timing as escalation rather than preparation: when ordinary means did not awaken David, God took an extraordinary course, pitying and preventing a man who had so horribly forsaken him. Henry draws the general rule: though God may suffer his people to fall into sin, he will not suffer them to lie still in it, and he seeks us before we seek him.

The choice of messenger is noticed by three of them, and the point is that he was not a stranger. Ellicott notes that Nathan was already intimate with David and recognised by him as a prophet (2 Samuel 7:4). Henry presses it two ways: David did not send for Nathan, though he never needed a confessor more, but God sent Nathan to David; and it was by this same hand that God had earlier sent notice of his kind intentions, so that the word in a minister's mouth must be received whether it speaks terror or comfort. He also credits the prophet with two refusals — not that David had sinned and so he would not come near him, nor that David was a king and he dared not reprove him.

On the parable itself Clarke declines to expound and explains why. Nothing in it requires illustration, its bent being evident, and it was framed to make David unwittingly pass sentence on himself; and he seals the point with a comparison to the previous chapter — the parable was in David's hand what his own letters had been in the hands of the brave but unfortunate Uriah. Wesley says the same without the parallel: Nathan prudently ushered in his reproof with a parable after the manner of the eastern nations, to surprise David and make him unawares give sentence against himself.
2:
How far the parable is an allegory is the first disagreement, and it is a disagreement about method. Ellicott denies that it is one: the story was designed to draw out David's indignation against the offender without being clear enough to awaken any suspicion of a personal application, and it alludes not to the special crimes of David but to the meanness and selfishness of the transaction — qualities which David was still in a condition to appreciate. He sets it beside two other parables used on kings to the same end (2 Samuel 14:2, 1 Kings 20:35). Gill, Wesley and Henry all read it the other way, assigning each element its counterpart. The many flocks and herds are David's wives and concubines, which Gill enumerates — six wives in Hebron, more taken after he came up from there, and besides these his predecessor's wives made over to him — while Wesley notes the same in a line.

The lamb is handled with equal particularity by those who allegorise. Gill makes it Uriah's one wife, much younger than her husband, and so a lamb, an ewe lamb, a little one; and he reports Abarbinel's further supposition that Uriah had been a widower with children by an earlier wife, the children of the parable, and was much older than Bathsheba. Wesley reads even the buying as a detail with a counterpart, the word being used as men then used to buy their wives, or else simply meaning that the man had procured her. Ellicott, who will not allegorise, nevertheless admires the workmanship, quoting the judgement that all these circumstances are exquisitely contrived to heighten the hearer's pity for the oppressed and his indignation against the oppressor. Henry pauses on the bare contrast of rich and poor before applying it, observing how unequally the world is divided and yet that infinite wisdom makes the distribution, so that the rich may learn charity and the poor contentment.

Clarke alone finds a flaw in the story. The lamb lying in the man's bosom can only mean that it was what we call a pet or favourite in the family; otherwise the circumstance would be very unnatural, and would most likely have prevented David from making the application he did, since it would have appeared absurd. It is, he says, the only part of this parable at variance with nature and fact — a judgement that treats the tale as a piece of invention to be tested rather than a figure to be decoded.

The traveller draws the most comment of any element, and two identifications are on offer. Gill reports that some understand Satan, who came to David and stirred up his lust by the temptations that offered, the word signifying a walker, one who goes about seeking whom he may devour and who is with good men only as a wayfaring man that does not abide with them; the Jews generally, he adds, understand it instead of the evil imagination or concupiscence in the man himself, the lustful appetite that wandered after another man's wife. Henry takes the second reading, citing it from the Jewish writers through Bishop Patrick, and then makes a grammatical observation that carries the whole point: the evil disposition is called a traveller because at the beginning it is only that, in time it becomes a guest, and in conclusion it is master of the house — for the one called a traveller at the opening of the verse is called a man, a husband, at its close. Yet he records the contrary observation too, that in David's breast lust was but as a wayfaring man tarrying for a night, and did not constantly dwell and rule there.
5:
The sentence David passes is harsher than the law allows, and Clarke is the one who says so. The phrase he uses means literally that the man is a son of death, a very bad man and one who deserves to die; but the law did not sentence a sheep-stealer to death at all, prescribing restitution of five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep (Exodus 22:1) — which is why David in the next breath orders the lamb restored fourfold, giving the legal penalty immediately after the illegal one. Gill accounts for the vehemence simply, by David's taking the story for a real fact.

What the anger proves is flatly disputed. Ellicott reads it as evidence that something in David had survived his sin: his generous impulses had not been extinguished, nor his warm sense of justice, and his naturally quick temper roused his indignation at once to the utmost (1 Samuel 25:22). Wesley reads the identical outburst as evidence of the opposite. The sentence was more than the fact deserved, or than David had commission to inflict, and it is observable that at the very time when he was most indulgent to himself and his own sin he was most severe and even unjust toward others — a pattern Wesley traces forward to the treatment of the Ammonites at the chapter's close, done, he notes, during the same impenitent continuance in sin. Henry takes Wesley's side with a gentler explanation: if the sentence be thought too severe, it must be imputed to the present roughness of David's temper, being under guilt and not having himself as yet received mercy.

The restitution has four different figures attached to it. Ellicott holds the Hebrew fourfold to be in exact accordance with the law, and points to the later instance of a man volunteering the same measure (Luke 19:8); he notes that most copies of the Greek read sevenfold and the Chaldee fortyfold, and judges both to have expressed more of human indignation than of law — David, he says, knew the law too well to change its terms. Gill reports a third enlargement from the grammar rather than the versions: Kimchi, taking the word as a dual, made the sentence eight lambs, twice the number the law commanded, on the ground that a rich man had stolen from a poor one, and Weemse renders it twice four on the rule that Hebrew doubles in the dual up to seven.

Keil and Delitzsch read the whole exchange as a trap that worked by not looking like one. The parable was so chosen that David could not suspect it had reference to himself, and with all the greater shock, therefore, did the prophet's three words fall on him. They also identify what the story was built to expose: just as the parable traces the sin to its root in insatiable covetousness, so the words of the LORD that follow bring out that same hidden background of all sins, and do it unsparingly, in order to press home the greatness of the iniquity and the condemnation it deserved.
7:
The three words are treated as the hinge of the chapter, and the commentary is mostly about their effect. Clarke calls it a terrible word, and says David appears to have been transfixed by it and brought into the dust before the messenger of God; he hears in it both halves of the sentence David had just passed turned back on him — thou art this son of death, and thou shalt restore this lamb fourfold. Gill supplies only the identification, that the man meant is the rich man of the parable. Wesley marks the change of footing in the speaker: Nathan now speaks not as a petitioner for a poor man but as an ambassador from the great God, which is Henry's phrasing almost word for word.

Ellicott uses the shock as evidence about the man who felt it. The boldness and suddenness of the application roused a slumbering conscience at once, and that, he argues, could not have happened had David been essentially a bad man. He was one whose main purpose in life was to do God's will, but who had yielded to temptation and then been entangled in further and greater guilt by the effort to conceal the first, his conscience all the while stupefied by the delirium of prosperity and power. What the three words did was bring what he had done suddenly before him in its true light. Ellicott sets the scene beside other prophetic rebukes of royal offenders, citing four such passages without expounding any of them.

Clarke pushes the fourfold restitution from the parable into the history, and flags his own doubt about doing it. Is it indulging fancy too much, he asks, to say that David was called in the course of a just providence to pay that fourfold debt by the untimely deaths of four sons — this child of Bathsheba, struck by the LORD; Amnon, murdered by Absalom; Absalom, slain in the oak by Joab; and Adonijah, put to death by order of his brother at the altar itself? Having raised the question he does not withdraw it, and he extends the reckoning further still: the sword and calamity did not depart from that house, from the murder of Amnon down to the slaughter of the sons of Zedekiah before their father's eyes; the daughter was dishonoured by her own brother, and the wives publicly defiled by his own son. His conclusion is put as two questions and an answer — who would repeat the transgression to share in its penalty, and can such conduct ever encourage anyone in sin? Surely not.
8:
The gifts are enumerated in order to make a point about ingratitude, and Ellicott states the purpose plainly: the prophet lists the chief favours shown to David so as to bring out not only his base ingratitude but the sheer unreasonableness of this particular sin. Henry reads the catalogue the same way and adds the clause about what was still in reserve — God was ready to bestow anything more to make him easy — drawing from it that where God has given much he yet gives more, and that his bounty is a great aggravation of our discontent and our desire of forbidden fruit. It is ungrateful, Henry says, to covet what God has prohibited while we have liberty to pray for what he has promised.

What "thy master's house" covers is read three ways. Gill rules out the palace at Gibeah and offers instead the household — wives, servants, wealth and riches, all confiscated through the rebellion that followed Saul's death — or else, as he prefers, the kingdom David succeeded to. Henry takes it as power over the house and household of his predecessor, and widens the plural, counting among David's former masters not Saul only but Nabal. Clarke reduces it to a single idea: perhaps the phrase means no more than that David was given absolute power over everything Saul had possessed.

The clause about the wives is the one that troubles them, and Clarke and Ellicott handle the trouble differently. Clarke takes the transfer as fact and explains it by custom: it was usual for a new king to succeed even to the wives and concubines, the whole harem of the deceased, and possession of them was a sure proof that he had obtained all regal rights. He then raises the obvious objection himself — could David, as Saul's son-in-law, take his father-in-law's wives? — and answers it by observing that delicacy was seldom consulted in such cases, with Absalom's public seizure of his own father's wives as the parallel, done precisely to show that he had seized the kingdom.

Ellicott doubts the fact rather than the propriety. The record names only one wife of Saul (1 Samuel 14:50) and one concubine, and that concubine was taken by Abner (2 Samuel 3:7); if Saul had others, David certainly could not have taken them until more than seven and a half years after Saul's death. On Ellicott's reading, then, the prophet is invoking the oriental custom by which a new king had a right to his predecessor's harem, rather than reciting something David had actually done — the gift named is an entitlement, not an inventory.
9:
The indictment uses two different verbs for the killing, and three of them notice it. Ellicott marks the second as a stronger word than the first, one that might well be translated murdered: it was murder in the eyes of the LORD, although accomplished indirectly by the sword of the Ammonites. Keil and Delitzsch make the same distinction and draw the structural conclusion — the repetition is no tautology but a sharpening, defining more exactly the manner in which David destroyed the man — and they add an aggravation the others do not, that the deed was done by the sword of the Ammonites, the enemies of the people of God. Clarke compresses the whole charge into a sentence: thou art the murderer, as having planned his death, and the Ammonite sword was thy instrument only.

Which commandment was despised is answered narrowly by Gill and broadly by Wesley. Gill names the law of God and in particular its sixth and seventh precepts, which David had shown no regard to and by breaking had slighted. Wesley, in words Henry uses almost exactly, takes the despised thing to be the word of the LORD, as the Hebrew has it — not the general commandment only but the particular word of promise sent earlier by this same prophet, that God would build him a house; had he valued that promise duly he would not have polluted his house with lust and blood. Wesley also presses the marriage itself as a distinct offence: to marry the woman he had defiled and whose husband he had slain was an affront upon the ordinance of marriage, making it not merely palliate such villainies but in a manner consecrate them.

The sentence on the house is where the three readings pull apart, though two of them arrive at the same place. Keil and Delitzsch insist that "for ever" must not be toned down to the vague idea of a long period but held firmly in its literal force; what they restrict instead is the other term, "thy house" meaning not David's line continued in his descendants but his household as it existed under him, until his death broke it up. Ellicott restricts the opposite word. The expression, in both its positive and negative forms, is constantly used to express the longest time possible in connection with whatever subject it governs, so that here it must mean as long as David lives. The two reach the same limit by incompatible routes, one by narrowing the house and one by relativising the forever.

Gill will not accept that limit at all. The sword did not depart during David's life, as appeared in the slaughter of two sons before his death and a third soon after, but it continued in his posterity through their wars with Israel and with other nations — an entail running past the grave rather than ending at it. On the fulfilment within David's lifetime all three agree, and they name the same three deaths: Amnon murdered by Absalom (2 Samuel 13:29), Absalom killed in his rebellion, and Adonijah executed at the last (1 Kings 2:25). Keil and Delitzsch add the principle that governs the whole sentence: the punishment answers to the sin.
11:
The sentence is spoken in the first person, and two of them convert it into permission. Clarke reads "I will take thy wives" as meaning that in the course of his providence God will allow all this to be done: had David been faithful, that providence would have turned it aside, but by his sin he has made his friend his enemy. Wesley glosses the giving in the same way, that God will by his providence give the man power over them. Gill prefaces the whole oracle with the point that Nathan was not speaking of himself but under a spirit of prophecy, which leaves the words as God's however their agency is construed.

That the punishment is cut to the shape of the sin is the governing idea, and Keil and Delitzsch set it out as a scheme. David's twofold sin was to be followed by a twofold punishment, each in an intensified form: for his murder he would have to witness murder committed in his own family, and for his adultery the violation of his own wives. They note the order too — his sin began in adultery and was consummated in murder, and the retribution runs the other way. Henry puts the same correspondence in a figure: as face answers to face in a glass, so does the punishment often answer to the sin, and here is blood for blood and uncleanness for uncleanness. He adds that this was the customary retribution for that offence, citing the imprecation in Job against the man who defiles his neighbour's wife (Job 31:10).

The oracle's vagueness is read as deliberate by Wesley and Henry alike. Neither the agent nor the manner is specified — the evil is to come out of David's own house, which Wesley takes as his own children and family, and the beneficiary is called simply a neighbour, one very near him. God expresses it darkly, Wesley says, so that the accomplishment should not be hindered; and Henry says the same, that it is not stated the thing would be done by David's own son lest the prediction being too plain should prevent its fulfilment. The phrase about his eyes Wesley reads not as sight but as certainty: David shall know it as surely as if he saw it, and shall be unable to hinder it. Both point forward to the same fulfilment, when the counsel of Ahithophel was carried out on the palace roof (2 Samuel 16:22), as Keil and Delitzsch do.

The contrast of secret and public closes the sentence, and the asymmetry is the sting. Gill describes the concealment in its stages: the adultery committed privately, the husband got killed in battle to hide it, and the marriage hurried on as soon as possible to cover the shame. Against that Keil and Delitzsch set the open repayment, before all Israel and in the face of the sun. Henry draws out what the publicity would cost beyond the act itself — the punishment being industriously proclaimed, David's sin in the matter of Uriah, though committed years before, would then be called to mind and commonly talked of on that occasion.
13:
The confession is four words long, and its brevity is taken as evidence rather than as a defect. Gill calls it short but full, arising from a thorough conviction of the evil and accompanied by real brokenness of heart and a sorrow after a godly sort. Keil and Delitzsch say the prophet's words went to David's heart and removed the ban of hardening that had pressed upon it, and they quote a comment that makes the shortness the point: the words are very few, as in the case of the publican in the Gospel (Luke 18:13), and that is a good sign of a thoroughly broken spirit — no excuse, no cloaking, no palliation, no searching for a loophole, no pretext, no human weakness pleaded, but guilt acknowledged openly and without prevarication. Henry says the same in his own terms, that David offers not a word to excuse or extenuate but owns the guilt and then aggravates it by naming against whom it was done. Ellicott sharpens the judgement by comparison: the very same words were used by Saul (1 Samuel 15:24), but in a totally different spirit, Saul's being a concession to the prophet made to secure his support and carrying no real penitence.

What the promise of life actually remits is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter, and there are three answers. Clarke denies outright that any pardon is being granted here. Many have supposed David's sin was now actually forgiven, which he calls perfectly erroneous: David as an adulterer stood condemned to death by the law, and all that Nathan is authorised to convey is that he shall not die a temporal death — he is to be preserved alive so that he may have time to repent, turn to God and find mercy. Wesley takes the narrower sense too, that the sin is put away so far as concerns David's own life, and that the death he escapes is the one his own sentence had earned. Against them, Ellicott makes the clause an assurance of forgiveness and nothing less. David had committed two capital crimes (Leviticus 20:10, Leviticus 24:17), but as an absolute monarch he had no reason to fear that any human authority would enforce the sentence; the divine word therefore matters to him far more as pardon than as the warding off of earthly danger, and the phrase is parallel to, and explanatory of, the putting away of the sin. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the verb the same way, as the LORD letting the sin pass by, that is, forgiving it. Henry gives a third answer by extending the death rather than narrowing the pardon: thou shalt not die means not die eternally, nor be for ever put away from God, the obligation to punishment being cancelled — which, he says, is the nature of forgiveness.

Clarke alone builds a doctrine of transfer out of the Hebrew. The verb, he renders, means that the LORD has caused the sin to pass over, or transferred it; and what was transferred, on his reading, is the legal punishment, which now falls on the child. He shall die, thou shalt not die — and Clarke takes the prophet's next sentence to be the direct information that this is what has happened.

The psalm composed on the occasion is used by both sides. Gill cites it as showing how full the short confession was, and Wesley sends the reader to it for the same purpose. Clarke turns it into an argument against them: if that psalm was written after this interview, as is generally supposed, then it is evident David had not yet received pardon when he composed it, since in it he is still confessing the crime in order to find mercy.
14:
The deed charged here is the whole series, not one act. Gill calls it a complicated wickedness — the adultery, the murder of the husband, and the occasioning of other men's deaths besides. What the blasphemy consisted in Henry supplies by putting the taunts into the mouths of the irreligious of that generation, who would triumph in the fall and speak ill of God and of his law: these are your professors, this is he that prays and sings psalms and is so very devout; what good can there be in such exercises if they will not restrain men from adultery and murder? And a second taunt about the unevenness of divine justice — was not Saul rejected for a lesser matter, and why then must David live and reign still?

Whether David can be blamed for other men's blasphemy is a question Henry raises and answers with a distinction. None have any just reason to speak ill of God or of his ways for David's sake, and it is their own sin that they do; yet he shall be reckoned with who laid the stumbling-block in their way and gave, though not cause, yet colour for the reproach (Romans 2:24). Henry adds that the damage has not expired with the generation that first took it: to this day there are those who reproach God, and are hardened in their own sin, through the example of David.

Why a public punishment should follow a granted pardon is where Ellicott states a general principle. Although David was forgiven, his sin had brought great scandal, and it was necessary that he should suffer the consequences publicly — important in his case both for the vindication of God's justice and to destroy the hope that other sins might also go unpunished, though the effect of sin generally is similar. The greater part of David's sufferings, Ellicott holds, came from what are called the natural consequences of his sin, flowing from it under the immutable laws of the world's moral government; and those laws are always in force, bringing home the earthly consequences of sin however fully the sinner has repented and been forgiven. Henry reaches the same place by a shorter road: God vindicates his honour by letting the world see that though he loves David he hates his sin.

That the stroke falls on the child is noticed as a difficulty by both. Henry states it as plainly as it can be stated — the guilty parent lives and the guiltless infant dies — and resolves it into sovereignty, all souls being God's, so that he may glorify himself in his creatures in what way he pleases; the landlord, as Henry puts it, may distrain upon any part of the premises he chooses. He also conjectures that the diseases and deaths of infants were less common then than now, which would make this, as an unusual thing, the more evident token of displeasure. Ellicott anticipates the opposite objection, that the death of one infant in the harem of a great eastern monarch might seem of small significance and a light punishment; David, he answers, saw it in its true light, as evidence of an unalterable purpose and a sign of the greater judgments still to come — and the people, no doubt, felt the appropriateness of it too.
15:
Nathan's departure is read as the close of a commission rather than a retreat. Gill has him go to his own house, probably in Jerusalem, having delivered his message, brought David to a sense of his sin and declared the forgiveness of it, and having nothing more from the LORD to say. Henry supposes he did not stay at court but went home to pray for the man he had been preaching to, and he finds in the whole errand an honour put upon the ministry, God making use of a prophet as the herald both of mercy and of judgment. Henry also traces what came of the prophet's name: David called one of his later sons by this same mother Nathan (1 Chronicles 3:5), and it was through that son, Henry notes, that the descent recorded in the third Gospel runs (Luke 3:31).

What David did when the prophet left is answered differently by two of them, and the difference matters for the chapter's chronology. Henry supposes he retired at that moment and composed the fifty-first psalm, in which, though already assured that his sin was pardoned, he still prays earnestly for pardon and laments the sin at length — for true penitents are most ashamed of what they have done when God is pacified toward them. Gill, dating the same psalm to the same occasion, had used it instead as proof of how complete that four-word confession was. Clarke, commenting a verse earlier, had used it to argue that no pardon had yet been received at all.

The striking of the child is reported in one clause and expounded in two directions. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the punishment just announced was inflicted without delay: when Nathan had gone home, the LORD smote the child so that it became very ill. Clarke reads the Hebrew of the sentence passed on it as describing a manner as well as a fact — dying he shall die — and takes it to mean that the child would lie in a dying state for seven days and then die, which is why the narrative says God struck it and it was very sick rather than that it died at once.

Henry alone turns the illness into an argument about human nature. The diseases and deaths of infants, who have not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression, and especially as they are sometimes so sadly circumstanced, he treats as sensible proofs of the original sin in which they are conceived. He guesses at the distemper — convulsions, perhaps, or some other dreadful disorder — without pressing the guess, and leaves the child's condition as the token of displeasure that David will spend the next verses trying to avert.
16:
Why David prayed at all, after being told plainly what would happen, is the question these verses force, and there are three answers. Three of them make the threatening conditional. Gill supposes that though the LORD had said the child should die, David might hope the sentence was conditional and that God would reverse it, and Wesley says the same in a line. Henry supplies the precedent, the reprieve granted to Hezekiah on his humiliation and prayer, and puts the hope as a question — who can tell whether God will yet be gracious to me? Clarke rejects the whole supposition. How could David pray so, he asks, after the solemn assurance he had received? The justice of God absolutely required that the penalty be exacted, either from the father or from the son, and this could not be reversed.

Ellicott moves the motive off the child altogether, endorsing a comment he takes from Otto von Gerlach. In a man whose penitence was so deep, the prayer for the child's preservation must have sprung from some other source than excessive love of a created object: his desire was to avert the stroke as a sign of the wrath of God, hoping to discern in the child's survival a proof of divine favour consequent upon his restored fellowship. When the child died he humbled himself under the mighty hand of God and rested satisfied with his grace, without giving himself up to fruitless pain. Having quoted that with approval, Ellicott adds a qualification of his own: David's deep love for the child is not to be overlooked altogether.

Where he went to pray is a flat contradiction between two of them. Gill has him go, perhaps, into the tabernacle he had built for the ark. Keil and Delitzsch rule that out, arguing from what the narrative says of his going up to the house of the LORD after the death that the coming here cannot have been into the sanctuary; it was into his own house or chamber, to pour out his heart before God and bend beneath the chastising hand. Wesley agrees with them, putting him in his closet.

The men who tried to lift him are described as two different kinds of people. Gill makes them some of the chief officers at court, charged with the management of his household, and Wesley the chief officers of his kingdom and household. Keil and Delitzsch, reasoning from the patriarchal usage, make them the oldest and most confidential of his servants, and pass on the gloss that they were the most highly honoured of them and those who had the greatest influence with him (Genesis 24:2).

What the fasting proved is answered at length by Henry and in a sentence by Wesley. Wesley denies that the excessive mourning proceeded simply from fear of losing the child, and traces it instead to a deep sense of sin and of the divine displeasure shown in the illness. Henry counts four marks of true repentance in it. David was willing to bear the shame of his sin, a living child being a continual memorandum of it, so that far from desiring its death as most in such a case would, he prayed for its life. He showed a tender and compassionate spirit, above what is commonly found in men of war toward little children even their own, and those who are penitent will be pitiful. He showed a concern for another world, interceding while the child was still within the reach of prayer chiefly that its soul might be safe and that his own sin might not come against it. And he showed a holy dread of God, deprecating the death above all as a token of anger against his house, so that the child's life would have been to him a token of reconciliation.
18:
Which seventh day is meant divides them two against two, and Gill is the only one who argues for his reading. He takes it as the seventh day from the child's birth, not from the onset of the illness, and gives his reason: it cannot be thought that David should have fasted seven days together. Henry counts the same way, having the child die when it was seven days old. Wesley takes the other view in four words, dating the seventh day from the beginning of the distemper; and Clarke, glossing the sentence passed earlier, had already read the Hebrew as meaning that the child would lie in a dying state for seven days and then die, which puts him with Wesley.

On Gill's and Henry's reckoning a further consequence follows, and Henry draws it. A child dying on the seventh day died before the eighth, and so was never circumcised; and Henry allows that David might perhaps have read this as a further token of displeasure, that the child went out of the world before being brought under the seal of the covenant. He does not let the inference stand against the child, however, since the benefits of the covenant do not depend upon its seals, and he says David did not on that account doubt its being happy.

The servants' silence is explained by their fear of what the news would do to him. Keil and Delitzsch give their reasoning as they put it to one another: while the child was still living they had spoken to him and he would not hearken, so how should they tell him now that it was dead — the worry being, as Keil and Delitzsch gloss it, that he would do himself an injury in the depth of his anguish. Henry reads the same fear as a misjudgement, the servants judging of David by themselves and concluding that he would then disquiet himself most of all, so that he did not learn of it until he asked. Gill fills in the physical scene that gave him away: they said these things to one another in a low voice so that he should not hear, though he was in the same room with them.

What David read in the whispering is agreed. Keil and Delitzsch have him see at once what had happened and put the question only for confirmation, so that the answer told him nothing he had not already understood.
20:
The three acts are read as one gesture, the formal laying aside of mourning. Keil and Delitzsch list them so — he washed, anointed himself and changed his clothes, that is, laid aside all the signs of penitential grief — and Gill notes only the detail that he rose from the floor on which he had been lying. Henry adds the motive behind the change of dress: he called for clean linen that he might decently appear before God in his house. Clarke supplies a comparative observation instead of an explanation, noting that bathing, anointing the body and changing the apparel are the first outward signs among the Hindoos of coming out of a state of mourning or of sickness.

Where he went next is given its identification. Keil and Delitzsch take the house of the LORD to be the holy tent upon Mount Zion; Wesley calls it simply the tabernacle. The reading matters because they had just denied that David's earlier praying took place there, so the going up now is a change of place as well as of posture.

What he went there to do is itemised by Wesley and by Henry, and their lists overlap without matching. Wesley gives five purposes: to confess his sin before the LORD, to own his justice in the stroke, to deprecate his just displeasure, to acknowledge the rich mercy that had spared his own life, and to offer such sacrifices as were required in such cases. Henry gives four, two of which are Wesley's: to acknowledge the hand of God in the affliction and humble himself under it, to submit to his holy will in it, to thank God that he himself was spared and his sin pardoned, and to pray that God would not proceed in his controversy with him nor stir up all his wrath.

Henry alone presses the propriety of worshipping at such a moment, and he does it by precedent and by maxim. The precedent is Job, who worshipped on hearing of the death of his children; the maxim is that weeping must never hinder worshipping, and that the afflicted man's business is to pray. He reads the meal that follows in the same key — David went to his own house and refreshed himself as one who found benefit from his religion in the day of affliction, for having worshipped he did eat, and his countenance was no more sad.
21:
The servants' question is not about the facts, as Gill is careful to note. They knew perfectly well what David had done; what they asked after was the meaning of it, the reason for such conduct and behaviour. Gill's gloss on David's answer is equally short: while the child was yet alive there was hope it might be continued.

Clarke makes the answer the occasion for a general claim about how threatenings were understood under the old dispensation, and the claim sits oddly against what he had said six verses earlier. David, and indeed all others under that dispensation, were so satisfied that God's threatenings and promises were conditional that even in the most positive declarations of judgment they sought for a change of purpose. So notwithstanding the plain words of Nathan about the child's death, David sought its life, not knowing but that the sentence might depend on some unexpressed condition — earnest prayer, fasting, humiliation — and in these he continued while there was hope; when the child died he ceased to grieve, seeing that grief must now be fruitless. This, Clarke concludes, appears to be the sole reason of David's importunity. It is worth setting beside his own earlier objection, that the justice of God absolutely required the penalty and that the sentence could not be reversed.

Henry turns the same answer into a rule for prayer that does not depend on settling the question. While the child was alive David thought it his duty to importune the divine favour toward it, since for all he knew the threatening might be conditional. From that Henry draws a licence: God gives us leave to be earnest with him for particular blessings out of confidence in his power and general mercy, even where we have no particular promise to build on. We cannot be sure, and yet let us pray, for who can tell but God will be gracious to us in this or that particular. His summary is a pair of clauses — while there is life there is hope, and while there is hope there is room for prayer.
23:
The first half of David's reason is read the same way by everyone. Gill makes it the plain futility of continuing — to fast and pray now answers no end that can be thought of. Henry puts the principle behind it: those who are dead are out of the reach of prayer, and our tears cannot profit them, since we can neither weep nor pray them back to this life. He notes the one apparent exception in David's own history, that he fasted and wept for Jonathan after his death, and distinguishes it as done in honour of the dead rather than in hope of recovering him.

The second half divides them four ways, and the division is about how much David believed. Keil and Delitzsch endorse a paraphrase of Clericus as very correct, and it is the barest possible reading: I shall go to the dead, the dead will not come to me. Ellicott names that reading in order to refuse it. Taken as mere words the clause might be the expression of a Stoic's comfort, he allows, but David in his whole nature and belief was as far as possible from being a Stoic, and in his mouth the words can scarcely be anything but an expression of confidence in a life of consciousness beyond the grave, and in the future recognition of those loved on earth.

Clarke occupies a middle position by separating two questions. It is not clear, he says, whether David was here expressing faith in the immortality of the soul: going to him may mean only that he too will die and be gathered to his fathers, as the child has been. But whether David expressed it or not, Clarke adds, we know the thing itself to be true, and he calls it one of the most solid grounds of consolation to surviving friends that they shall by and by be joined to those they have lost in a state of conscious existence — a doctrine with a powerful tendency to alleviate the miseries of human life, without which grief would in many cases wear out its subject before it wore out itself.

To show how far that consolation reaches, Clarke goes outside Scripture for it. He quotes at length a passage of Cicero in which Cato speaks of the happy day when he shall quit this impure and corrupt multitude and join the divine company of souls who have left the earth before him, finding there not only the illustrious men he has named but his own son, than whom none better was ever born; he had laid that son's body on the pyre whereon the son ought rather to have laid his, and yet the soul has not left him but has gone before into a country where he saw he should soon rejoin it. Clarke's point is that even the heathen drew comfort from expecting to meet their friends in conscious existence, and he closes by recalling who has taught us not to sorrow for departed friends as those who have no hope.

Henry takes both senses at once rather than choosing. David goes to the child first to the grave, and the consideration of our own death should moderate our sorrow at the death of our relations, since whatever we lose of them now we shall shortly die and go to them. And he goes to the child secondly to heaven, to a state of blessedness which even the Old Testament saints had some expectation of; from which Henry concludes that godly parents have great reason to hope concerning children that die in infancy that it is well with their souls, the promise being to us and to our seed.
24:
Gill notices that this is the first place where Bathsheba is called David's wife, and reconstructs what she needed comforting about. She was greatly disconsolate over the sin she had committed, the divine displeasure, and the child's death as its token — and, Gill adds, she may have had a scruple whether it was lawful to go on living with David at all. The comfort offered was accordingly doctrinal: that God had pardoned the iniquity and would give them another son to succeed him and build a house for his name. Wesley names the same two causes, her former sin and her loss. Henry draws out what the sequel settles: though the marriage had displeased the LORD, David was not commanded to put her away — so far from it that God gave him by her the son on whom the royal covenant would be entailed. Clarke alone keeps the reproach in view, observing that David's extraordinary attachment to this beautiful woman was the cause of all his misfortunes.

The name is explained three ways. Keil and Delitzsch make it a pledge rather than a description: David named the child so because he took his birth as an assurance of being again a partaker of peace with God — and they expressly deny the other derivation, that it referred to the Ammonite war being over when he was born. Clarke takes it prophetically, the word signifying peaceable and there having been almost unbroken peace throughout the reign. Henry declines to choose, giving three reasons at once: the birth was a token of God's being at peace with them, the prosperity entailed on the child, and his being a type of the prince of peace.

On when the birth actually happened, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree against the order of the narrative. Ellicott argues that it could hardly have fallen before the capture of Rabbah, since the siege is unlikely to have occupied two years, and that it stands here, after the custom of Scripture narrative, to close the story of Bathsheba in its proper connection. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion in a clause, that in all probability Solomon was not born until the Ammonite war had ended.

Who sent by the hand of Nathan is genuinely unclear, and Gill lays out three constructions before preferring one. Either David sent by him to Bathsheba to acquaint her with the child's name, which Gill thinks unlikely; or David delivered the child into Nathan's hand to be brought up in the nurture of the LORD; or, as Gill prefers, the LORD sent word by Nathan to David that he loved Solomon. Wesley finds a like ambiguity in the closing clause, which may mean either because of the LORD's love to the child or because the LORD commanded the name.

The second name puzzles Clarke and is explained away by Ellicott. Clarke recalls no other instance of a minister of God being employed to name a servant's child, and finds it strange that the father's name was the one that prevailed. Ellicott removes the strangeness by denying that the second name was ever meant as a title: it does not appear to have been intended to do more than express the divine acceptance of Solomon, and it never came into use as a personal name. Henry reads it as doctrine instead. Though the parents were a seed of evil-doers, the covenant was so well ordered that it took away all attainder of blood, signifying that those by nature children of wrath should by grace be not merely reconciled but made favourites. He adds the pattern he sees in the exchange: God removed one son and gave another in his place, as Seth was given instead of Abel (Genesis 4:25), often balancing the griefs of his people with comforts in the very thing wherein he has afflicted them.
26:
The siege is agreed to belong earlier than its place in the narrative. Gill says it can hardly be thought Joab lay before Rabbah long enough for David to have two children by Bathsheba, and explains the arrangement: the account of the finishing is set here so that the story of Bathsheba might lie together without interruption. Henry judges it most probable that the conquest was effected a good while before, soon after Uriah's death, perhaps during the days of Bathsheba's mourning for him. Ellicott marks the same point from the other side, noting that the parallel narrative is resumed here (1 Chronicles 20:2).

That Joab takes the city and then asks David to come and take it is an apparent contradiction, and all three who raise it solve it the same way. Clarke puts the difficulty sharply — how can Joab have taken the royal city and then send for David to come and take the city? — and answers that Rabbah was composed of a city and a citadel: the former, containing the king's residence, Joab had taken, and expecting to master the latter shortly he sent for David. Ellicott distributes the three expressions accordingly, the royal city of one verse and the city of waters of the next both meaning the town proper, while the city of the verses that follow is the citadel, more strongly fortified. Keil and Delitzsch read the capital as the city excepting the acropolis, and say the next verse makes this clear by calling what was captured the water-city. Both describe the ground: a narrow valley of the upper Jabbok with the town on both banks, shut in by bare hills of moderate height and, on Keil and Delitzsch's measure, no more than two hundred paces across, the northern height crowned by the ancient acropolis.

What made it the city of waters is explained four ways. Clarke takes it for the city where the tank or reservoir stood that supplied the town and suburbs, and Henry says the same, adding the military consequence that cutting off the supply would oblige the rest to surrender speedily. Wesley gives a different reason altogether, that Rabbah was so called because it was encompassed with water. And Clarke reports a reading that changes the sense of Joab's message rather than the name: some would translate the Hebrew not as having taken the water-city but as having intercepted or cut off the city's waters, which is how Houbigant renders it and how Josephus describes the operation — on which construction Joab's urgency is explained, since a citadel deprived of water could not hold out long.

Why Joab sent for the king at all is given two different characters. The text's own reason is self-protective: lest he take the city himself and it be called after his name, which is how Clarke reports it. Henry reads the same act as honourable, holding that Joab acted honestly in sending for David to come in person and complete the action so that he might have the praise of it, showing himself a faithful servant who sought his master's honour and his own only in subordination to it. Keil and Delitzsch add a practical reason the others do not: David gathered all the people, meaning the men of war who had stayed behind in the land, from which it appears that Joab's besieging force had been considerably weakened by the length of the siege and the taking of the water-city.

Henry alone pauses on the oddity of the victory being granted at all. God might justly have made the sword of the Ammonites, which David had misused to kill Uriah, a standing plague to him and his kingdom; instead he breaks it and makes David's own sword victorious — and does so, Henry observes, before David repents, so that this goodness might be what leads him to repentance.
28:
Why the whole army should be called up for what remained is answered with two reasons, and the commentators are not sure which applies. Ellicott puts them side by side: Joab proposes a general muster of the forces still in the land either because additional strength was genuinely needed to take the citadel, or simply so that the formal capture should be made by David in person. Wesley holds that no additional strength was needed — having taken one part of the city, Joab concluded the remaining part could not long stand out — and reads the stated motive bluntly, lest the honour of taking it fall to him.

Gill adds a third purpose that neither of the others mentions. The men David gathered served partly to recruit Joab's troops, who by the length of the siege and the enemy's sallies against them might be greatly diminished, and partly to make conquests of the other Ammonite cities and carry off their spoil — so that the muster looks beyond Rabbah to the campaign the chapter's last verses describe.
30:
Whose crown it was draws a small textual note and a dismissal. Keil and Delitzsch read "their king" as the king of the Ammonites and infer from the crown being taken off his head that he had either been taken prisoner or slain at the capture of the city. Gill names him as the king who had so shamefully abused David's ambassadors, now fallen into his hands and stripped of the ensigns of royalty. Ellicott notes that the same Hebrew letters which give "their king" would also spell the name of the chief Ammonite idol, and reports that some writers have on that ground supposed the idol's crown to be meant — a supposition he calls quite unnecessary.

The weight is the real problem, and there are four ways out of it. Keil and Delitzsch compute the Hebrew talent at three thousand shekels, which they reckon at some eighty-three pounds, and then object on physical grounds: the strongest man could hardly bear such a crown on his head for however short a time, and David could scarcely have set it on his own. Their solution is to distrust the figure — the account of the weight rests not on actual weighing but on an approximate estimate, which is somewhat too high.

Clarke and Wesley keep the figure and change what it measures. Both observe that the word may signify either weight or price, in Hebrew as in Greek and Latin, and both find the decisive argument in the clause that follows: precious stones are never valued by the weight of gold, so the verse must be reckoning worth rather than mass. On Clarke's calculation the crown with its jewels came to a little over five thousand pounds sterling, which he thinks the true sense; Wesley adds the same objection Keil and Delitzsch raise, that the weight would be too great either for the Ammonite king or for David to wear.

Ellicott changes the unit instead of the reckoning. If the Hebrew weights are meant the amount is extraordinary, the silver talent being above a hundred pounds and the gold talent twice as much; but various other eastern talents were in use, the Babylonian and the Persian among them, of much smaller weight, and it is not unlikely that a light talent was current among the Ammonites. Clarke reports a fourth figure of the same kind, Whiston's talent of only seven pounds, on which David might have carried the crown on his head with little difficulty. Ellicott, however, concedes what all four solutions leave standing: on any reasonable supposition the weight would still have been too great for the crown to be worn commonly.
31:
Who the people were is the first mitigation on offer, and two of them take it. Gill denies that all the inhabitants are meant and limits the victims to the Ammonite princes — the counsellors who had advised the shameful usage of David's ambassadors, and others who had expressed satisfaction in it. Wesley argues the same from the grammar: the word is indefinite and need not mean the whole people, but the men of war and especially the chief actors in that villainous business and in the war that followed, for which they deserved severe punishment. Keil and Delitzsch grant no such limit, stating flatly that he had the inhabitants executed, and with cruel tortures.

The decisive question is textual, and one letter is emended in opposite directions. The Hebrew as it stands says David put the people into the saw, which Keil and Delitzsch judge to yield no appropriate sense; they read the verb instead as "he cut them in pieces," bringing the verse into line with Chronicles (1 Chronicles 20:3). Ellicott makes the same correction, holding that no doubt a single letter should be changed to agree with that parallel. Clarke changes the letter the other way. He observes that the two words differ by part of one character, that this chapter's manuscripts show no variant favouring the Chronicles reading, and that six or seven manuscripts collated by Kennicott carry the milder word even in Chronicles. His conclusion is that David made the people slaves and set them to work — sawing, making iron harrows or mining, hewing wood and making brick — and that sawing asunder and hewing human beings have no place in the text.

The instruments and the furnace are explained by those who keep the harsher sense. Ellicott identifies the iron harrows as heavy tools, often armed with sharp points beneath, used for threshing grain and breaking straw. On the last clause he defends the received text — the brick-kiln is what the Hebrew says, and there is no sufficient reason to question it — while reporting that the margin reads a proper name instead, on which some have supposed David made the Ammonites pass through the very fire by which they used to consecrate their own children. Wesley adopts that marginal reading and finds the justice of it: they were punished with their own sin, and with the punishment they had inflicted on their children. Keil and Delitzsch decline to fix the second instrument at all, the word occurring only here and the usual rendering of axes resting on nothing but the use of the same root for felling trees.

On David's conduct the verdicts divide along the same line as the text. Henry grants that putting to the sword in the heat of battle all whom he found in arms would have been severe enough, but holds that killing them afterwards in cold blood by cruel tortures did not become the man who on taking the government had promised to sing of mercy as well as judgment; had he made examples only of those who abused his ambassadors it might have passed for necessary justice. As it is, he calls it a sign that David's heart was not yet made soft by repentance — he had not yet found mercy, or he would have been readier to show it. Wesley reaches the same judgement and dates it, supposing David did this while his heart was still hardened and he was bereaved of the Spirit that would have taught him more mercy. Ellicott neither excuses nor condemns but historicises: David acted according to the customs and knowledge of his time, and abhorrent as these things are to the spirit of Christianity, he and his contemporaries took them as matters of course, without a suspicion that they were not in accordance with God's will.
